newsitem.title: FINLAND: LIPPONEN SEES SDP COUNCIL EMU DECISION AUTUMN 1997.
newsitem.headline: LIPPONEN SEES SDP COUNCIL EMU DECISION AUTUMN 1997.

text.p: Prime Minister and Social Democratic Party chairman Paavo Lipponen said at the weekend that the SDP council will not decide its stance on Finnish membership of EMU until next autumn.
"The social democratic party council will decide on the issue next autumn," Lipponen said in an interview published in regional newspaper Pohjalainen on Saturday.

On November 16, Lipponen told an SDP council meeting that it should rule on Finnish participation in the planned third stage of Europe's Economic and Monetary Union at an extraordinary council meeting in May-June, or September 1997.
In the interview, Lipponen repeated that Finland's final stance on EMU will be decided by parliament in the early part of 1998 -- at the same time with other EU countries.
He also said that all Finnish government parties should clarify by autumn their stance on EMU.
Lipponen repeated that there would be no separate Finnish referendum on EMU-membership.
"A referendum has been carried out alreay once. Then the Maastricht treaty was approved, which included plans for monetary union," Lipponen said.
Finns voted in October 1994 in favour of EU membership.

Addressing recent criticism against government policy from within the SDP, Lipponen said: "It would be very unfortunate if social democrats are so impatient that they don't realise this is a task for the long term."
Lipponen said the squabble within the party had been initiated by individual MPs.
"There is no conflict of interest between the party, me and the trade union-wing (of the party)," he said.

Lipponen said the key factor for improving employment was economic growth, and that the government's achievements had not been bad so far. But he admitted that current growth was not enough to stabilise the economy.
Lipponen saw scope for jobs creation in the service sector and said measures to cut labour costs should be considered, while at the same time ensuring an adequate disposable income for employees.
The left-right-green coalition's stated foremost goal is to halve unemployment to 8-9 percent by the end of its term in 1999.

New employment models are sought all the time and Lipponen said any measures to be introduced will be in line with the government programme and will not put new strains on government expenditure in supplementary budgets.
He also reiterated the government's commitment to low inflation and low interest rates.

Lipponen said the idea of a return to a government coalition between SDP and the Centre Party, recently floated by centrist chairman and ex-PM Esko Aho, was old-fashioned and reminded him of the hammer and sickle.
Lipponen said he was satisfied with the cooperation between the conservatives and SDP in the five-party government in office since April 1995.
But Lipponen said he was on good terms with Aho, the opposition leader, and that they meet regularly.
